source_evidence.observation: Dimensional splitting extends one-dimensional high-resolution methods to more dimensions through successive coordinate-direction problems. The source calls this the simplest extension under the stated grid condition, describes it as often surprisingly effective in practice, and refers to Section 19.5.

source_evidence.location: Raw PDF page 26; printed page 4; Section 1.1.1
source_evidence.anchor: Equation (1.10) and the paragraph beginning Each component of q
source_evidence.observation: For any two points x1 and x2, d/dt ∫ from x1 to x2 q(x,t) dx = f(q(x1,t)) − f(q(x2,t)). Each component of q is the density of a conserved quantity; its interval total changes only through endpoint fluxes. Source terms are needed when the quantity is not conserved.

source_evidence.location: Raw PDF pages 26–27; printed pages 4–5; Section 1.1.2
source_evidence.anchor: provided that q and f(q) are sufficiently smooth; At a discontinuity in q
source_evidence.observation: The differential equation follows from the integral equation under sufficient smoothness. Discontinuities may develop from smooth initial data. At a discontinuity, the PDE does not hold classically, whereas the integral conservation law remains fundamental and continues to hold.

source_evidence.location: Raw PDF page 27; printed page 5; Section 1.2, first paragraph
source_evidence.anchor: grid cells; cell average of q; numerical flux functions
source_evidence.observation: Finite volume methods approximate the integral over each grid cell, or its cell average obtained by dividing by cell volume. Each time step changes these values through edge fluxes. Numerical flux functions approximate the correct fluxes using the approximate cell averages.

source_evidence.location: Raw PDF page 27; printed page 5; Section 1.2.1
source_evidence.anchor: Equation (1.11); q_l = Q_{i−1} and q_r = Q_i
source_evidence.observation: A Riemann problem is a hyperbolic equation with piecewise constant initial data having one jump, illustrated at x = 0 with states q_l for x < 0 and q_r for x > 0. Neighboring cell averages provide these states, and the Riemann solution provides information for numerical fluxes and cell-average updates.

source_evidence.location: Raw PDF page 28; printed page 6; continuation of Section 1.2.1
source_evidence.anchor: the exact Riemann solution is often too expensive to compute for nonlinear problems
source_evidence.observation: Approximate Riemann solvers are used in implementing numerical methods because exact nonlinear Riemann solutions are often computationally expensive.

source_evidence.location: Raw PDF page 28; printed page 6; Section 1.2.2
source_evidence.anchor: shock-capturing methods; implicitly incorporate the correct jump conditions
source_evidence.observation: Shock capturing aims to represent discontinuities without explicitly tracking them. Discontinuities are smeared over one or more cells; successful methods should incorporate correct jump conditions, minimize smearing, and avoid nonphysical oscillations. High-resolution finite volume methods based on Riemann solutions often perform well.

source_evidence.location: Raw PDF page 28; printed page 6; Section 1.3, first paragraph
source_evidence.anchor: A Riemann problem normal to each edge; a Riemann problem normal to this plane
source_evidence.observation: One-dimensional Riemann problems are also used in multidimensional hyperbolic computations. In two dimensions, normal problems at edges of polygonal cells determine edge fluxes. In three dimensions, a cell face can be approximated by a plane, and a Riemann problem normal to that plane can compute its flux.

source_evidence.location: Raw PDF page 125; printed page 103; Section 6.3, first paragraph
source_evidence.anchor: combine the best features of both methods; Second-order accuracy is obtained where possible
source_evidence.observation: High-resolution methods combine the smooth-solution accuracy of second-order methods with the favorable monotone behavior of upwind methods. Second-order accuracy is sought where possible but is not insisted upon where the solution is not smooth.

source_evidence.location: Raw PDF pages 125–126; printed pages 103–104; Section 6.3, limiter discussion
source_evidence.anchor: applying some form of limiter; each wave limited independently from the others
source_evidence.observation: Limiters adjust the correction magnitude according to solution behavior. For systems, smooth and discontinuous waves may coexist; the stated ideal is accurate smooth portions and nonoscillatory discontinuous portions. Characteristic structure and Riemann waves allow second-order corrections with each wave limited independently.

contract_plain_english: For a rectangular or logically rectangular finite volume grid, LeVeque presents dimensional splitting as the simplest extension of one-dimensional high-resolution methods to more dimensions: solve one-dimensional problems successively along each coordinate direction. The source describes this fractional-step approach as often effective in practice and refers to Section 19.5, without specifying a splitting schedule or proving accuracy, stability, or conservation of the composed method in the selected paragraph [raw PDF p. 28, printed p. 6, Section 1.3]. The inherited setting uses cell averages updated through numerical approximations to physical fluxes, with integral conservation remaining fundamental at discontinuities [raw PDF pp. 26–27, printed pp. 4–5, Sections 1.1.1–1.2]. High-resolution terminology seeks second-order accuracy where possible while accommodating nonsmooth solution portions, including characteristic-wave limiting for systems; it does not impose second-order accuracy everywhere [raw PDF pp. 125–126, printed pp. 103–104, Section 6.3].
